The Western quoll (Dasyurus geoffroii) was once widespread across much of arid and semi-arid Australia, but its distribution has contracted considerably since European colonisation. Females give birth to altricial young following a brief gestation period of 16 days [tg = 16 days] when measured at a core body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a remarkably short intrauterine phase typical of many dasyurid marsupials. This species produces one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], with each litter containing six pups [N_R_i = each litter containing six pups], a reproductive output that reflects the energetic constraints of a medium-sized carnivorous marsupial. The tiny neonates weigh a mere 0.011 grams [Wwb = 0.011 grams] at birth, representing one of the smallest relative birth masses among mammals and an extreme manifestation of the altricial developmental strategy characteristic of the family Dasyuridae.

Like most marsupials, the young of the Western quoll undergo a prolonged period of dependency within the maternal pouch before transitioning to nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning has been recorded as 158 days [tx = 158 days] at a maternal body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a duration during which the pups undergo substantial morphological development and begin to consume solid prey items brought by the mother. Juveniles are entirely dependent on milk during the early stages of pouch life, but gradually increase their intake of invertebrates and small vertebrates as the weaning period progresses. By the time of nutritional emancipation, the young have developed the full dentition and locomotor capabilities required for independent foraging, though they may still associate with the mother for several weeks thereafter while refining their hunting skills.

Adult females of this species attain a maximum recorded body mass, often referred to as the ultimate wet weight, of 890 grams [Wwi = 890 grams], a value that places Dasyurus geoffroii among the smaller members of the genus. This body size is associated with a life history strategy that balances moderate reproductive investment against the challenges of an unpredictable environment. Sexual maturity is reached relatively early in life, with the time since birth at puberty documented as 365 days [tp = 365 days] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], meaning that females born in one breeding season are capable of reproducing in the following year. This rapid maturation is advantageous in a landscape where rainfall and prey availability can be highly variable, allowing the population to respond quickly to favourable conditions.

The lifespan of the Western quoll in natural habitats has been estimated at approximately 6.2 years [am = approximately 6.2 years] at a core body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], based on a combination of mark-recapture studies and observations of captive individuals. This longevity is comparable to that of other medium-sized dasyurids and reflects a relatively slow pace of life for a mammal of this body mass. Mortality rates are highest during the juvenile and early sub-adult stages, with predation by introduced foxes and cats representing a significant source of attrition in many populations. Those individuals that survive to adulthood may experience multiple breeding seasons, though reproductive senescence has been noted in older females, manifesting as reduced litter sizes and lower pup survival rates.

An understanding of the reproductive physiology of Dasyurus geoffroii is essential for conservation management, particularly in reintroduction programs. The maximum reproductive rate, inferred from a combination of litter size and breeding frequency, amounts to a single litter of six pups per year, with each litter containing six pups [N_R_i = each litter containing six pups] and one litter produced annually [F_R_i = one litter produced annually] under the thermal conditions typical of this endothermic species (36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]). Translocation projects in Western Australia have demonstrated that individuals translocated to predator-free reserves exhibit breeding success comparable to that of source populations, with females producing litters within the first year of release. Ongoing monitoring suggests that the species can maintain stable populations in suitable habitat provided that threats from introduced predators and habitat fragmentation are effectively managed.
